Le 23 mai dernier au parc Martin Luther: On May 23, a gathering took place at Martin Luther King Park: a community soup kitchen organized by the Comité d’action Côte-des-Neiges contre la pauvreté, which brought together various community organizations from the neighbourhood. The organizers came together to denounce the provincial government’s inaction in the face of rising poverty across Quebec, and especially in the neighbourhood. Among those present, some share their concerns with us.
Malgré le soleil tapant de la mi-mai, un: Despite the blazing mid-May sun, a good hundred people gathered to take part in the awareness activities put together by the network of organizers. Soup and hot meals are handed out for free on site, an initiative of Multicaf, a community cafeteria located right across from the park and taking part in the event.
De nombreuses personnes attendent de se: Many people wait to be served a hot meal offered by the community cafeteria Multicaf.
Phat Nguyen est arrivé au Québec en 1980: Phat Nguyen arrived in Quebec in 1980. After fleeing Vietnam in the wake of the boat people exodus, he spent six months in a refugee camp in Malaysia, waiting for an answer to the asylum applications he had sent to several Western countries. In the end, it was Canada that opened its arms to him, and where he settled at 18.
Ses yeux, qui paraissent fatigués, sont: His eyes, which look tired, are almost hidden by the cap that shields his face from the beating sun. He takes the time to sit down at one of the park’s outdoor tables before he starts telling us his story, and why he is here today.
Il est un bénéficiaire de longue date de: He has been a Multicaf regular for a long time. “I always come here, because it lets me eat for less,” he says, in a voice so weak it is hard to make out over the music playing from the speakers. “If I go to the grocery store or eat out, I can easily pay around five to ten dollars per meal. Here, I buy a card for 20 meals for $35,” he explains. “It’s become harder and harder to pay for groceries, but also rent and basic needs. And that’s not even counting the unexpected, urgent expenses that come with life,” he laments.
Habitant de Parc-Extension, le sexagénai: A resident of Parc-Extension, the man in his sixties has worked as a janitor for several years. Having lived in his neighbourhood for more than twenty years, he has seen how the rising cost of living and housing has affected the people around him. “I see more and more people on the street who can’t pay their rent anymore. I have friends who had to leave their homes because they couldn’t pay on time,” he says, eyes lowered.
Aujourd’hui, il est là au titre de bénéf: Today, he is here as a user of the community cafeteria, but also as a citizen concerned about inflation and poverty. “I think the government should put more money into affordable housing, everywhere but especially in the neighbourhoods where people are increasingly being put out on the street,” he says. “I also believe the minimum wage has to go up, because you can’t survive on $15.75 an hour, especially when you have kids like I do.”
Même à l’autre extrémité du parc, on peu: Even at the other end of the park, you can hear this phrase ring out between each of the speeches given by community representatives. It is aimed, among others, at the provincial government, which the organizations blame for its inaction on poverty.
« À Côte-des-Neiges, la pauvreté est amp: “In Côte-des-Neiges, poverty is amplified by systemic barriers and other factors of exclusion, such as isolation or a lack of support networks, not knowing about the neighbourhood’s resources, and so on,” Tasnim Rekik, one of the gathering’s organizers, begins firmly. Wearing a long black veil that covers her hair and falls over her shoulders, she has an even stronger presence. “Over the past few years, the pandemic and its economic fallout have weakened populations that were already vulnerable, such as seniors, immigrants with children and other people who are recent immigrants or have precarious status,” she lists into the microphone, her voice booming through a large speaker.
C’est dans ce contexte que les organisme: It is in this context that the organizations present at the park, such as Multicaf, the Comité de logement du quartier, the Collectif pour un Québec sans pauvreté and the Centre des travailleurs immigrants, took the floor, to name just a few.
Des représentants d’organismes communaut: Representatives of the neighbourhood’s community organizations speak to ask the government for concrete measures against poverty.
« La pauvreté n’a plus la même image qu’: “Poverty doesn’t look the way it did ten or even five years ago,” says Jean-Sébastien Patrice, executive director of Multicaf. “Today, it’s people who get up in the morning and drop their kids off at daycare before going to work forty hours a week. They’re the ones who are poor and who aren’t being heard, despite all the effort they put in to make ends meet,” he laments.
Cette différence, monsieur Patrice et le: Mr. Patrice and the Multicaf workers have had a front-row seat to this change: “A few years ago, we served about 1,200 people a year at the community cafeteria. Today, more than 9,000 people need low-cost meal services to get by,” he says, dismayed by this new reality.
Être au bord du gouffre pour bénéficier: Having to be at the edge of the abyss to get help
Les organismes présents en sont certains: The organizations present are certain: you can’t talk about poverty without talking about the government’s lack of action. “To be eligible for social assistance, a recipient must have less than $887 in their account. The government demands that people be at the edge of the abyss before they can ask for help,” denounces a representative of Projet Genèse, an organization that fights for social and economic rights in Notre-Dame-de-Grâce.
« Une fois que tu es en situation vulnér: “Once you’re in a vulnerable situation, you have to go through a whole process to get access to help. These delays, for people who are already in an unstable situation, create even more poverty. They create destruction. With all that waiting, it becomes practically impossible for people to keep going,” he explains. Meanwhile, the reality of life and its costs quickly catch up with the most vulnerable.
Une fois la demande d’aide sociale reçue: Once a social assistance application is received, and if it is approved, the benefit amounts granted no longer keep up with the cost of living, according to Projet Genèse. “For an adult recipient, it can amount to a meagre $807 a month. With inflation and rent prices that just keep exploding, who can live on a sum like that?” he asks the people present, who nod in approval.
« On demande simplement au ministère de: “We’re simply asking the Ministry of Health and Social Services not to leave people in misery,” he concludes, his sentence interrupted by cheers and applause.
Le Centre des travailleurs et travailleu: The Centre des travailleurs et travailleuses immigrants de Montréal (CTI), based in Côte-des-Neiges, is also on hand. One of its representatives highlights a key fact: “Nearly 30% of the Côte-des-Neiges population works full time but is still below the poverty line, according to <l1>a study completed in 2006</l1>.” Recent figures on the neighbourhood’s economic situation paint an equally chilling picture. <l2>In 2016, the median income for single people in Côte-des-Neiges was $24,687; for households, it was $41,498.</l2>
Sur place, on entend aussi que les immig: It is also said on site that immigrants are hit harder by poverty. “When a worker is an immigrant, they face more obstacles. Newcomers tend to end up in underpaid jobs even though they’re often overqualified in their fields. For many employers, immigration is a form of labour that’s easier to exploit and more cheap,” he says in one breath. “The uncertain legal status of many puts them in a very vulnerable position, where it’s harder for them to complain or defend themselves in cases of abuse of power by employers.”
Il ne s’agit plus d’une question démogra: It is no longer a general demographic question, he believes, but a provincial problem. “Our premier keeps saying that asylum seekers shouldn’t have access to subsidized daycare, yet he doesn’t complain when those same daycares <l1>employ these people for next to nothing to fill staffing shortages</l1>,” he criticizes, addressing the Legault government.
Ça n’est pas anodin pour le collectif «: It is no coincidence that the “Côte-des-Neiges contre la pauvreté” collective chose to gather on May 23. Last year, on the same date, nearly 1,000 people gathered in front of the National Assembly in Québec City to demand a real plan to fight poverty.
Cette année encore, le « Collectif pour: This year again, the “Collectif pour un Québec sans pauvreté” spoke up to call for concrete, structural measures to fight poverty. Among them: a sufficient social income so that everyone can live with dignity, access to universal public services, an increase in the minimum wage, and campaigns to combat prejudice about poverty.
« La pauvreté n’est pas une fatalité. On: “Poverty is not inevitable. We can get out of it, we’re able to fight this. It’s not the means that are lacking, but the political will,” says a representative of the collective Regroupement national contre la pauvreté.
« On invite le gouvernement à nous prouv: “We invite the government to prove us wrong, but unfortunately, the latest plan to fight poverty is disappointing. It proposes no concrete measures, no increase in social assistance benefits or the minimum wage, no reduction in fees, no investment in public services,” he laments. He is referring to the <l1>third plan to fight poverty</l1> tabled in 2023.
Le collectif ne perd toutefois pas espoi: The collective has not lost hope, however. “There’s still time to adopt an ambitious plan against poverty,” he concludes, followed by a burst of applause. By the end of June, Chantal Rouleau, the minister responsible for Social Solidarity and Community Action, is expected to table a fourth plan to fight poverty. The ministry has also set up, over the same period, a <l1>public consultation period</l1> to better understand the population’s needs in terms of poverty.
Si le soleil tape de moins en moins fort: As the sun beats down less fiercely and the afternoon draws to a close, the soup kitchen line does not shrink. Multicaf’s volunteers keep serving one and all, until they have nothing left to give.
Malgré le brouhaha de la petite foule qu: Despite the hubbub of the small crowd that has built up during the gathering, you can hear the representatives of “Côte-des-Neiges sans pauvreté” repeat their demands: “Let’s create environments that foster development. Let’s create lively, interesting environments; not just for the wealthiest, but places where there are challenges and where people want to grow in love and respect, but above all in dignity. Really listen to us this time!”
